content.title: Interpolating Values in Science Datasets
content.overview: Interpolation is the process of estimating an unknown value that falls between two known data points within a measured range. On the ACT Science section, this requires identifying the correct 'bracketing' points and applying linear reasoning to find a precise estimate.
learning_objectives: Distinguish between interpolation (inside the data range) and extrapolation (outside the data range).
Identify the two data points that immediately surround a target input value.
Calculate an interpolated value using the bracket-and-linear method.

sections.title: Understanding Interpolation
sections.content: Interpolation is used when a question asks for a value not explicitly listed in a table or plotted as a point on a graph, but which exists within the boundaries of the existing data. Unlike extrapolation, which predicts trends beyond the known data, interpolation stays within the 'brackets' of measured points. The ACT assumes a linear relationship between these two closest points for the purpose of estimation.

sections.title: The Bracket-and-Linear Method
sections.content:
To interpolate accurately, follow these three steps: 1. Locate the Brackets: Find the nearest measured x-value below your target (x1) and the nearest measured x-value above your target (x2). Note their corresponding y-values (y1 and y2). 2. Calculate the Fractional Distance: Determine how far the target is between x1 and x2 using the formula: Fraction = (Target - x1) / (x2 - x1). 3. Apply to Y: Multiply this fraction by the difference in y-values (y2 - y1) and add the result to the starting y-value (y1). The formula is: y = y1 + [Fraction * (y2 - y1)].

![A flowchart showing the steps: Identify Brackets, Calculate Fraction, Multiply by Y-Difference, Add to Y1.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/0c542019-6fae-4f3e-8e35-341df4e80824-1786506593300-396.webp)

sections.title: Verification and Logic Checks
sections.content: Always perform a 'sanity check' on your result. First, ensure your calculated fraction is between 0 and 1. If it is not, you have likely chosen the wrong bracketing points. Second, ensure your final interpolated y-value falls numerically between y1 and y2. If the data shows a decreasing trend, your interpolated value should be lower than y1 but higher than y2.

worked_examples.question: A study measures the solubility of a salt at various temperatures: 10°C (20g/L), 20°C (35g/L), 30°C (55g/L), and 40°C (80g/L). Based on these data, what is the estimated solubility at 25°C?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify bracketing points for 25°C. These are 20°C (x1=20, y1=35) and 30°C (x2=30, y2=55). Step 2: Calculate the fraction. (25 - 20) / (30 - 20) = 5 / 10 = 0.5. Step 3: Apply to y-values. The y-difference is 55 - 35 = 20. Multiply by the fraction: 0.5 * 20 = 10. Add to y1: 35 + 10 = 45. The estimated solubility at 25°C is 45g/L.

common_mistakes: Using the wrong bracketing points (e.g., using the first and last points of a table instead of the two closest to the target).
Confusing interpolation with extrapolation by trying to predict values outside the measured range.
Failing to account for a decreasing trend, where the y-difference (y2 - y1) will be negative.
Simple averaging of the y-values when the target x is not exactly at the midpoint (0.5) of the x-interval.
exam_tips: If the target x-value is exactly halfway between x1 and x2, you can simply average y1 and y2.
Check the units on the axes or table headers to ensure your interpolated value matches the required units.
On graphs, use a straightedge or the edge of your answer sheet to visually align the target x-value between the two known points.
content.recap: Interpolation estimates values within a known data range by identifying the two closest surrounding points and calculating the proportional distance between them. The resulting value must always fall between the two known y-coordinates.

knowledge_claims.content: Interpolation is the estimation of a value that lies between two known, measured data points within a dataset.
Interpolation differs from extrapolation because interpolation occurs within the range of measured data, while extrapolation occurs outside it.
The first step in interpolation is identifying the 'bracketing points,' which are the immediate lower and higher measured x-values surrounding the target.
The fractional distance of a target x between two points x1 and x2 is calculated as (Target - x1) / (x2 - x1).
The linear interpolation formula for y is y = y1 + [Fraction * (y2 - y1)], where the fraction represents the target's relative position between x1 and x2.
A valid interpolated y-value must always fall numerically between the y-values of the two bracketing points.
If the calculated fraction for interpolation is less than 0 or greater than 1, the chosen bracketing points are incorrect for the target value.
When the target x-value is exactly at the midpoint of the x-interval, the interpolated y-value is the arithmetic mean of y1 and y2.
In a decreasing data trend where y2 is less than y1, the y-difference (y2 - y1) used in the interpolation formula will be a negative number.
A common error is using the global average of all data points instead of the specific local slope between the two closest bracketing points.
Interpolation is required when an ACT Science question asks for a value at an input (like 35°C) that is not explicitly listed in a table containing 30°C and 40°C.
Linear interpolation assumes that the rate of change between two adjacent data points is constant.

Researchers placed two groups of equal-sized leaves from the same plant species in chambers. They exposed the leaves to blue light or red light at the intensities shown and measured net carbon dioxide uptake after 8 minutes. Positive uptake indicates that photosynthesis exceeded respiration.

According to the figure, what was the value for Blue light at the x-axis value 100?
items.explanation: Read the requested series at the specified x-value.

videoLesson.title: Interpolate Within Two Data Points
videoLesson.description: Recognize the two surrounding datapoints and their coordinates on a table or graph. Use linear bracket interpolation by computing the fractional distance and applying it to y values.
